data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Trained non-expert panels using explicit checklists outperform single experts on verifiable tasks only when the checklist encodes the diagnostic cues the expert would use implicitly; the reliability gain is mechanistic, driven by preventing cue-omission under cognitive load.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the checklist omits a cue the expert uses tacitly (e.g. configural cue interaction), panel mean accuracy can fall below expert accuracy.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the task is perceptual rather than propositional (e.g. radiology, wine tasting), checklist compliance may degrade signal by forcing verbal proxies.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If non-experts are untrained on cue definitions, checklist items are interpreted idiosyncratically, inflating variance.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Expert intuition operates as a fast pattern-matcher that typically recapitulates a cue-list, but under noise, fatigue, or base-rate pressures it omits cues. The checklist forces sequential, accountable cue sampling; aggregating across non-experts then cancels individual cue-sampling errors, yielding lower variance than a single expert whose cue omission is systematic within that one trial.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
